title: Why Your $100 Keeps Shrinking (Inflation Explained)

youtube.title: Why Your $100 Buys Half of What It Did (Inflation Explained)
alt_titles: Inflation Is a Hidden Tax. Here's Who Pays It
Where Did Half Your Money Go? Inflation, Simply Explained
youtube.hook: Inflation explained simply: a $100 bill from 2000 buys about half as much today. Where did the other half go, and who secretly wins from it? Dave finds a $100 bill in an old jacket. Nobody touched it, yet it lost half its value. We explain inflation with ducks and bread: why prices rise, the 2022 spike, who wins and who loses, shrinkflation, the craziest hyperinflations in history, and how people try to protect their money.

beats.text: Dave is cleaning his closet. And in an old jacket, he finds something amazing.
A one hundred dollar bill. From the year two thousand.
Nobody stole it. Nobody spent it. Nobody even touched it.
But today, that bill buys only about half of what it bought back then.
Half of Dave's money just... vanished. Without leaving the jacket.
Today: where the other half went, who wins and who loses, why governments actually want a little of this, and how people try to protect themselves.
This invisible thief has a name. Inflation.
Inflation means prices go up over time. Which is the same as saying: each dollar buys a little less.
The government measures it with a giant shopping basket. Food, rent, gas, clothes, doctor visits, phone bills. Thousands of prices, checked every month.
A basket that cost one hundred dollars in two thousand costs about one hundred and ninety four dollars today.
Prices almost doubled. So Dave's hundred dollar bill now buys what about fifty two dollars bought back then.
The bill didn't shrink. The world around it got more expensive.
So why do prices go up? Let's go back to our little town.
The town has one hundred loaves of bread, and one hundred dollars.
Now imagine everyone suddenly gets more money. But the bakery can't bake more bread that fast.
More money chasing the same bread. People compete. The baker raises the price.
That's reason one: too much money, not enough stuff.
Reason two: things get harder to make. If the flour becomes expensive, or the truck that delivers it gets stuck, bread costs more too.
And reason three: expectations. If everyone expects prices to rise, workers ask for higher pay, and shops raise prices early. It can feed itself.
This isn't just theory. We all lived through it.
In twenty twenty, the pandemic hit. The government sent out relief money, and the Federal Reserve cut interest rates to almost zero.
The amount of money in the economy jumped by roughly forty percent in about two years.
At the same time, factories closed, ships got stuck, and supply chains broke. Then energy prices spiked.
More money. Fewer things. Classic recipe.
In June twenty twenty two, inflation hit nine point one percent. The highest in more than forty years.
Here's something most people never think about. Inflation doesn't hurt everyone the same way.
Losers first. Anyone holding cash. Grandma's savings under the mattress lose value every single year.
People on fixed incomes, whose pay doesn't go up, can afford less and less.
Now the surprise winners. Borrowers.
Remember Dave's mortgage? His payment is fixed at about two thousand dollars. If prices and wages go up, those two thousand dollars get easier to pay.
And the biggest borrower of all? The government. With forty trillion in debt, inflation quietly makes that debt smaller compared to the whole economy.
That's why some people call inflation a hidden tax. It moves value from savers to borrowers. Without anyone voting on it.
So why not just aim for zero inflation?
Because the opposite is scary too. It's called deflation. Prices falling.
Sounds great, right? But if prices keep falling, people wait to buy. Why buy a TV today if it's cheaper next month?
Shops sell less. Companies cut jobs. People spend even less. The economy can freeze.
So the Federal Reserve aims for a small, steady inflation of about two percent a year. Like a gentle breeze, not a storm.
And when inflation gets too hot, it uses brake number three from our first video. It raises interest rates.
In twenty twenty two and twenty twenty three, it raised them from almost zero to over five percent. Loans got expensive. Borrowing slowed. And inflation cooled down.
Now, companies found a clever trick. Sometimes, the price doesn't go up at all.
Instead, the bag of chips gets a little smaller. The chocolate bar gets a little thinner. Same price. Less stuff.
This is called shrinkflation. And the official numbers actually try to track it, by counting the price per ounce, not per bag.
So next time your cereal box looks a little lonely inside, now you know why.
Here's something the headlines don't tell you. Your inflation might be different from the official number.
The official number is an average basket. But if you rent, and your rent went up fast, your inflation felt much higher.
If you drive a lot, gas prices hit you harder. If you work from home, maybe less.
That's why the news can say three percent, while your wallet feels like it's screaming.
So look at your own basket. Where does your money actually go every month? That's your real inflation.
Now, three percent a year sounds small. But some countries have seen inflation so extreme, it sounds made up.
In Germany, in nineteen twenty three, prices rose so fast that by November, a single loaf of bread cost about two hundred billion marks.
Workers were paid twice a day, and ran to the shops before their money lost value by the afternoon.
Children played with stacks of banknotes like building blocks. The paper was worth more as a toy than as money.
And in Zimbabwe, the government printed a one hundred trillion dollar bill. It still wasn't enough for a bus ride.
And America? Much calmer. But over a long time, small inflation adds up. What cost one dollar in nineteen thirteen costs about thirty three dollars today.
Slow. Quiet. But relentless. That's why understanding it matters.
So how do people protect themselves from the invisible thief? A few common ideas. This is education, not advice.
One. Don't let too much cash just sit. Money in a regular account earning almost nothing loses value every year.
Two. Some savings accounts and government bonds pay interest that tries to keep up with inflation. Some are even linked to it directly.
Three. Over long periods, things like businesses and property have often grown faster than inflation. But they can also fall, sometimes a lot.
And four. Your income is your biggest weapon. If prices rise five percent and your pay rises zero, you got a pay cut. Even if nobody said it.
So let's recap.
One. Inflation means each dollar buys less. Since two thousand, prices have almost doubled.
Two. It comes from too much money, things getting harder to make, and expectations.
Three. It hurts savers and helps borrowers. And the Fed aims for about two percent, not zero.
Now, for thousands of years, when people feared their money was losing value, they ran to one thing.
A shiny yellow rock that you can't eat, can't drive, and can't live in. And yet it's worth trillions.
Why is gold so expensive? That's next. Subscribe, and check your old jackets.
